evidence_legend.verified: The claim was confirmed on an official vendor/project documentation page actually fetched during this research pass (2026-10-23); the exact URLs are in the entry's sources.
evidence_legend.proposed: The claim comes from the Phase 1 spec, the 2026-10-23 catalog proposal, a search-result snippet, or researcher inference, and was NOT confirmed on a fetched official page. Proposed claims must not be enforced as compatibility rules until verified.

tools.name: ROS 2
tools.purpose: Middleware framework and library ecosystem for building robot applications; the base layer other ROS tools run on.

platforms.detail: Tier 1 for ROS 2 Jazzy per REP 2000 (full unit/CI/packaging testing).
Tier 1 for ROS 2 Humble per REP 2000.
Tier 1 for both Jazzy and Humble per REP 2000.
Tier 3 only (community reports, no dev-team testing) for Jazzy and Humble per REP 2000.
Tier 2 (periodic CI) per REP 2000.

detection.detail: Existence of /opt/ros/<distro>/setup.bash (e.g. /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash, /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash); after sourcing, $ROS_DISTRO names the distro. This /opt/ros layout and sourcing step are what Nav2's and Gazebo's official install docs both build on.
ros2 --version and sourcing checks from the Phase 1 spec sketch (spec-sourced; the string was not confirmed on a fetched docs.ros.org page in this pass because docs.ros.org blocked fetching).
apt packages ros-<distro>-desktop / ros-<distro>-ros-base (names seen only in search-result snippets of the blocked docs.ros.org install page).

version_constraints.rule: Distro-to-Ubuntu pairing: Jazzy targets Ubuntu 24.04, Humble targets Ubuntu 22.04 (REP 2000 Tier 1).
Support windows per REP 2000: Jazzy May 2024 - May 2029; Humble May 2022 - May 2027.
REP 2000 dependency floors for Jazzy: Gazebo Harmonic, C++17 minimum, Python 3.8 minimum language requirement (Ubuntu Noble ships Python 3.12.3).

tools.name: Gazebo
tools.purpose: 3D robotics simulator (Gazebo Sim) with its own library suite; runs standalone and integrates with ROS 2 via ros_gz.

platforms.detail: Gazebo Jetty (recommended) and Gazebo Harmonic (recommended if using ROS 2 Jazzy) per the official get-started matrix.
Gazebo Harmonic (recommended) and Gazebo Fortress (recommended if using ROS 2 Humble). Harmonic binaries are provided for Jammy and Noble via packages.osrfoundation.org.
Gazebo Harmonic (recommended) and Fortress per the official get-started matrix.
Support via Conda-Forge is 'not fully functional, as there are known runtime issues' per official docs.

detection.detail: apt metapackage gz-harmonic installs all Harmonic libraries on Ubuntu (per-release metapackages follow the same gz-<release> pattern).
The gz sim executable is the launch/detection entry point after install; note Fortress uses a different command, ign gazebo, instead of gz sim.
With ROS 2 integration installed: apt package ros-<distro>-ros-gz present under /opt/ros/<distro>.

version_constraints.rule: Official ros_gz pairing table: Jazzy<->Harmonic and Humble<->Fortress are the recommended pairings; Kilted<->Ionic; Lyrical/Rolling<->Jetty.
Incompatible per the official table: Jazzy with Fortress, Ionic, or Jetty; Humble with Ionic or Jetty.
Lifetimes: Harmonic (LTS) EOL May 2029; Fortress (LTS) EOL May 2027.

depends_on.why: The ros_gz bridge integrates Gazebo with ROS 2 under the official pairings; Gazebo is an independent project and runs standalone without ROS 2.

tools.name: RViz2
tools.purpose: 3D visualizer for ROS 2 data (topics, TF, robot models); ships as a ROS 2 package, not a standalone product.

platforms.os: Same platforms as the installed ROS 2 distro
platforms.detail: RViz2 releases are published per ROS distro (humble, jazzy, kilted, lyrical, rolling on the ROS index), so its platform support is the distro's REP 2000 tier matrix.

detection.detail: ROS package rviz2 present in the sourced distro (package directory under /opt/ros/<distro>/); the ROS index lists per-distro rviz2 releases (e.g. 11.2.29 for Humble, 14.1.24 for Jazzy at research time).

version_constraints.rule: RViz2 versioning is locked to the ROS 2 distro: each distro carries its own rviz2 version series, and RViz is part of the official ROS 2 repos file installed via the ROS 2 installation instructions.

The common claim 'RViz2 is included in the ros-<distro>-desktop install variant' could not be confirmed verbatim from a fetched official page (docs.ros.org blocked fetching); treat desktop-variant membership as unconfirmed.

depends_on.why: RViz2 is a ROS 2 package from the official ROS 2 repos and only runs inside a sourced ROS 2 environment.

tools.name: Nav2
tools.purpose: Autonomous navigation framework for mobile robots (planning, control, localization, behaviours) delivered as a ROS 2 package stack.

platforms.os: Platforms of the underlying ROS 2 distro
platforms.detail: Nav2 publishes per distro (Humble: Maintained, Jazzy: Active Support, Kilted: Maintained, Rolling: Development per its docs) and states no separate OS matrix; binary packages exist for Humble, Jazzy, Kilted and Rolling per the official build docs (pre-built Docker images listed for the same set).

detection.detail: apt/ROS packages ros-$ROS_DISTRO-navigation2 and ros-$ROS_DISTRO-nav2-bringup installed for the sourced distro (e.g. ros-jazzy-navigation2 under /opt/ros/jazzy/).
Alternative source install: a colcon workspace (e.g. ~/nav2_ws) containing the navigation2 checkout built against $ROS_DISTRO.

version_constraints.rule: Nav2 branches and binaries are organised by ROS distro; the default branch for Rolling is main, and Nav2 does not release binaries on Rolling (source build required there).

depends_on.why: Every official Nav2 install/build path starts by sourcing /opt/ros/<distro>/setup.bash; Nav2 is a ROS 2 package stack.
Nav2's simulation quickstart runs a TurtleBot in Gazebo; navigation on a real robot needs no simulator.
Nav2 docs offer pre-built Docker images and dev containers as an alternative install route, never a requirement.

tools.name: PX4 Autopilot
tools.purpose: Open-source autopilot flight stack for drones and other autonomous vehicles; developed as a source checkout and built locally (incl. SITL simulation).

platforms.detail: The Ubuntu LTS versions supported by PX4 per its dev-environment docs; CI/release target is 24.04, build tests also run on 22.04; Ubuntu 26.04 is explicitly not yet supported.
PX4 macOS dev environment builds for Pixhawk/NuttX hardware and Gazebo simulation; CI exercises Apple Silicon only. No macOS version number is named in the docs.
Supported only as Ubuntu Linux running inside WSL2 (default Ubuntu 22.04; 22.04 and 24.04 options), not a native Windows toolchain.

detection.detail: A recursive git checkout of PX4-Autopilot (github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot) with the dev environment set up via Tools/setup/ubuntu.sh (or macos.sh).
Built SITL binary at build/px4_sitl_default/bin/px4 inside the checkout (the path PX4's own Gazebo simulation docs invoke).
arm-none-eabi-gcc --version is PX4 docs' own toolchain verification for the NuttX build toolchain installed by the setup script.

version_constraints.rule: PX4's supported and recommended ROS 2 platform is ROS 2 Jazzy LTS on Ubuntu 24.04; on Ubuntu 22.04 use ROS 2 Humble LTS instead.

ROS 2 applications must use px4_msgs with the same message definitions as the firmware; from PX4 v1.16 (message versioning) a different version is possible only with the ROS 2 Message Translation Node running.
PX4's Ubuntu dev setup installs Gazebo Harmonic by default; on Ubuntu 24.04 Gazebo Harmonic, Ionic and Jetty are supported, and modern Gazebo supersedes Gazebo Classic for Ubuntu 22.04 onwards.

depends_on.why: PX4 SITL's current default simulator is Gazebo (installed by the dev setup), but PX4 builds and flies without it and other SITL modes exist.
Only needed for ROS 2 companion-computer integration over uXRCE-DDS; the autopilot and its SITL do not require ROS 2.

tools.name: QGroundControl
tools.purpose: Ground-control station application for flight control, vehicle setup and mission planning for PX4/ArduPilot (MAVLink) vehicles.

platforms.detail: Supported versions per the Stable V5.1 download page; installers for x86_64 and Arm64.

Stable V5.1 download page; universal binary (Apple Silicon + Intel), signed and notarized, installed by dragging QGroundControl to Applications. Note: the master/daily docs raise this floor to macOS 14.4 or later.
AppImage downloads (x86_64 and aarch64) run on these versions; Ubuntu 22.04 is possible only by building QGC yourself.
Supported per the Stable V5.1 download page (arm 32/64 APK).

detection.detail: Linux: an executable QGroundControl AppImage file (QGroundControl-<arch>.AppImage) — the official Linux distribution form.
macOS: QGroundControl.app in the Applications folder (drag-installed from the official .dmg).
Windows: presence of the installed application from the official installer executable; the fetched docs do not state a Windows install path, so the exact location is unconfirmed.

version_constraints.rule: QGC's own guidance: a computer with at least 8 GB RAM, an SSD, Nvidia or AMD graphics and an i5 or better CPU suits most applications.
Linux pre-install requirements per the download page: user in the dialout group for serial access, and libfuse2 plus XCB libraries for the AppImage.
No QGC command-line version flag is documented on the fetched official pages; do not rely on a --version probe for QGC.

tools.name: MAVSDK
tools.purpose: Library/SDK for programmatic control of MAVLink systems: a C++ library plus language wrappers (Python package on PyPI, Swift, Java, others). It is NOT a standalone application.

platforms.detail: MAVSDK describes itself as cross-platform across these systems (v1.0 guide introduction).

platforms.os: Python wheels: Linux x86_64 and aarch64 (incl. 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS); macOS x86_64 and arm64; Windows x86, x64 and arm64
platforms.detail: Wheel availability per the Python quickstart; explicitly no wheels for 32-bit ARM Linux (armv6/armv7) — use mavsdk-grpc or a 64-bit OS there.

detection.detail: Python package metadata for the PyPI package mavsdk in the active environment (e.g. pip show mavsdk) — the check is the standard pip-metadata probe for the package the quickstart installs with pip install mavsdk; the literal command is not printed in MAVSDK's docs.
C++ form: the libmavsdk-dev .deb installed on Ubuntu, or the Homebrew formula mavsdk on macOS, per the C++ quickstart's install routes.

version_constraints.rule: Python form requires Python 3.8 or later.
C++ examples must match the installed MAVSDK version's branch (e.g. check out branch v2 for an installed v2.x.y).

depends_on.why: MAVSDK needs a MAVLink system to talk to and its docs use a running PX4 SITL as the test target, but any MAVLink autopilot works and the library installs standalone.

tools.name: Docker
tools.purpose: Container platform in two forms: Docker Engine (daemon + CLI, native on Linux) and Docker Desktop (application bundling the engine for macOS/Windows/Linux).

platforms.os: Ubuntu 26.10 / 26.04 LTS / 24.04 LTS / 22.04 LTS (64-bit; x86_64, armhf, arm64, s390x, ppc64le)
platforms.detail: Docker Engine supported Ubuntu versions per the official Engine install page; Ubuntu derivatives such as Linux Mint are not officially supported.
Docker Desktop on Linux system requirement per the official Desktop install page; installs to /opt/docker-desktop.

platforms.os: Windows 10 64-bit 22H2 (build 19045) / Windows 11 64-bit 23H2 (build 22631) or higher, WSL 2.1.5 or later, 8 GB RAM
platforms.detail: Docker Desktop on Windows requirements per the official install page; Desktop is not supported on Windows Server versions.

platforms.os: macOS: current and two previous major releases; at least 4 GB RAM
platforms.detail: Docker Desktop on Mac support rule per the official install page; separate Apple silicon and Intel downloads; installs as /Applications/Docker.app.

detection.detail: docker info (alias docker system info) succeeding against a running daemon distinguishes an operational Docker from a CLI-only install — the classic installed-but-not-configured false positive.
Linux Engine packages docker-ce, docker-ce-cli, containerd.io, docker-buildx-plugin, docker-compose-plugin present (the .deb set installed by the official Engine instructions).
Docker Desktop install locations: /Applications/Docker.app (macOS), /opt/docker-desktop (Linux), %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\DockerDesktop (Windows per-user install).

version_constraints.rule: Conflicting unofficial packages (docker.io, docker-compose, podman-docker, etc.) must be uninstalled before installing Docker Engine.
Docker Desktop commercial use in enterprises over 250 employees or over $10M annual revenue requires a paid subscription (stated on the official Desktop install pages).

tools.name: Visual Studio Code
tools.purpose: Free, open-source code editor application; language toolchains and robotics extensions are user-installed add-ons, not bundled.

platforms.os: Windows client (64-bit); download requires Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit)
platforms.detail: Per the official requirements and download pages.

platforms.os: macOS versions with Apple security update support (typically latest release and two previous)
platforms.detail: Stated as a rule, not a numbered version, on the official requirements page.

platforms.os: Linux (Debian): Ubuntu Desktop 20.04, Debian 10; Linux (Red Hat): RHEL 8, Fedora 36
platforms.detail: Per the official requirements page; Linux additionally needs GLIBC 2.28+ and GLIBCXX 3.4.25+.

detection.detail: code --version (documented as -v/--version in the official CLI reference, printing version, commit and architecture). On macOS the code command is on PATH only after running the Shell Command: Install 'code' step.
Windows user-setup install location %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Microsoft VS Code.

version_constraints.rule: Recommended hardware per official requirements: 1.6 GHz or faster processor, 1 GB RAM; download under 200 MB, disk footprint under 500 MB.

tools.name: PlatformIO
tools.purpose: Embedded development platform: PlatformIO Core (CLI, command pio) plus PlatformIO IDE extensions — the recommended route is the VS Code extension; projects select boards and frameworks (Arduino, ESP-IDF, others) per environment in platformio.ini.

platforms.os: Windows, macOS, Linux (via the VS Code route)
platforms.detail: PlatformIO IDE is built on VS Code, which its docs describe as available for Windows, macOS and Linux; the Core installer script documents a Windows flow and terminal flows for other systems. A formal Core host-OS support list was not stated on the fetched pages.

detection.detail: pio --version (equivalently platformio --version) — --version is listed in PlatformIO Core's official CLI guide.

Standalone Core lives in a Python virtual environment at core_dir/penv (installer-script installs); the VS Code extension route bundles Core inside PlatformIO IDE, so absence of a standalone pio does not prove absence.

version_constraints.rule: Linux IDE route requires the python3-venv package for a smooth PlatformIO experience (docs' wording).
Arduino framework selection in platformio.ini (platform = espressif32, framework = arduino, board = esp32dev) is shown in the official VS Code integration docs.

Selecting ESP-IDF inside PlatformIO as framework = espidf for the espressif32 platform: seen only in a PlatformIO Registry example (search result, not a fetched docs page), so treat the exact framework key as unconfirmed in this pass.

depends_on.why: PlatformIO IDE is an extension built on VS Code and is the recommended route, but PlatformIO Core CLI installs and runs standalone without it.

tools.name: ESP-IDF
tools.purpose: Espressif's official IoT development framework/SDK for its own ESP32-family chips: API libraries and source plus the idf.py build/flash tooling and toolchains.

platforms.detail: Get Started hardware requirements: a computer running Windows, Linux, or macOS; current installs use the ESP-IDF Installation Manager (EIM) with per-OS pages. Legacy (v5.2-era) prerequisites are documented for Ubuntu/Debian, CentOS 7 & 8, Arch, and macOS via Homebrew/MacPorts.
Full setup guides verified for ESP32-C5 (latest) and ESP32-P4 (v5.2), with install.sh target examples esp32, esp32s2 and 'all'; no single exhaustive chip list was confirmed on one fetched page.

detection.detail: Checkout at ~/esp/esp-idf with environment activation via . ~/esp/esp-idf/export.sh; tools live under $HOME/.espressif by default (IDF_TOOLS_PATH overrides). This is the legacy flow that was default before ESP-IDF v6.0; current installs may instead be EIM-managed (eim / eim-cli command present).
After sourcing export.sh, idf.py resolves and runs (idf.py set-target / build / flash are the documented project commands). The specific flag idf.py --version was not stated on a fetched page.

version_constraints.rule: Python 3.11 is the minimum supported version for ESP-IDF (latest Linux setup page).
CMake 3.16 or newer is required (v5.2 setup docs).
The ESP-IDF build system does not support spaces in the paths to ESP-IDF or to projects.

depends_on.why: OpenOCD is the JTAG debug server in ESP-IDF debug flows; building and flashing firmware do not require a standalone OpenOCD.

tools.name: Arduino IDE
tools.purpose: Arduino IDE 2 desktop application for writing, compiling and uploading sketches; board support arrives via installable Board Packages/cores, not built in.

platforms.detail: Per the official IDE 2 download/install guide.
Distributed as an AppImage 64 bits (X86-64); FUSE must be installed (e.g. libfuse2 on Ubuntu 22.04+).
Per the official IDE 2 download/install guide; installed by copying the downloaded file into the Applications folder.

detection.detail: Presence of the installed IDE 2 application per OS: the copied application in the macOS Applications folder, the installed Windows application, or the executable Linux AppImage file. The exact bundle/binary name was not stated on the fetched official pages.

version_constraints.rule: Target-board support is add-on only: boards are installed through the IDE's Board Manager as Board Packages.

tools.name: STM32CubeIDE
tools.purpose: STMicroelectronics' C/C++ IDE application for STM32 MCUs/MPUs (Eclipse-based variant; a VS Code-based variant launched 2025 is now ST's focus). Bundles GNU Arm toolchain, STM32CubeProgrammer CLI and debug servers.

platforms.os: Windows 10 / 11 (64-bit only); Ubuntu LTS 22.04 and 24.04, Fedora 43 (Linux); macOS 15 (Sequoia) and 26 (Tahoe)
platforms.detail: Per ST's installation guide UM2563 Rev 7 (Feb 2026): only 64-bit OS versions supported; 2 GB RAM minimum (4 GB recommended), 6 GB free disk (15 GB for OpenSTLinux MPU work).

detection.detail: Debian/RPM package presence: ststm32cubeide_<version>_amd64.deb / .rpm installed via ST's deb_bundle.sh / rpm_bundle.sh installers.

Installed application presence: STM32CubeIDE in the macOS Applications folder (dragged from the official .dmg), or the installed program location on Windows/Linux; no CLI --version for the IDE is documented.

version_constraints.rule: ST's own documents disagree on supported OS versions: UM2563 Rev 7 lists Ubuntu LTS 22.04/24.04 and Fedora 43, while release note RN0114 (CubeIDE v2.2.0) lists Ubuntu LTS 26.04 and Fedora 44 (both list Windows 10/11 and macOS 15/26). Version-pin any platform claim to a specific CubeIDE release before enforcing it.
In current 2.x releases STM32CubeMX is detached from the CubeIDE integration (RN0114 records the v2.0.0 detachment): CubeMX is a companion tool, not a bundled component.

tools.name: Zephyr
tools.purpose: Open-source RTOS delivered as source, with the west meta-tool (Python CLI) managing workspaces/build/flash/debug, and the Zephyr SDK providing per-architecture toolchains and host tools.

platforms.os: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and later, macOS, Windows (host)
platforms.detail: The Getting Started guide sets up a command-line environment on Ubuntu, macOS or Windows and covers Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and later; the Zephyr SDK bundle supports Linux, macOS and Windows (Linux bundles for x86_64 and aarch64 hosts).

platforms.os: 500+ target boards across ARC, ARM, RISC-V, x86 and more
platforms.detail: Target breadth per the Zephyr Project FAQ and SDK architecture list.

detection.detail: A west workspace (conventionally ~/zephyrproject) with west installed in its Python venv (~/zephyrproject/.venv): west is only on PATH when the venv is activated, per the Getting Started guide.
Zephyr SDK extracted as ~/zephyr-sdk-<version> (or another documented root) with setup.sh run, or ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR pointing at the install; alternatively installed via west sdk install.
west --version as a probe: the fetched west docs state west --help / west -h but not --version, so this common probe is unconfirmed against fetched docs.

version_constraints.rule: Host dependency minimums per Getting Started: CMake 3.28.0, Python 3.12 (strongly recommended; newer Python may fail on some systems), devicetree compiler 1.4.6.

Each Zephyr version has a recommended Zephyr SDK version; the exact pairing numbers live in the Zephyr SDK Version Compatibility Matrix, which was not fetched in this pass — do not enforce specific SDK-version pairings yet.

depends_on.why: The Zephyr SDK bundles its own OpenOCD build used to flash and debug Zephyr applications; a standalone OpenOCD is an alternative source of the same capability, not an added requirement.

tools.name: OpenOCD
tools.purpose: Open On-Chip Debugger: a debug-server CLI that provides JTAG/SWD debugging, in-system programming and boundary-scan testing for embedded targets via a debug adapter; GDB connects to it.

platforms.os: Host OS list not confirmed from OpenOCD's own fetched pages
platforms.detail: The fetched User's Guide pages describe target/adapter support, not a host-OS support matrix; in practice OpenOCD most often arrives bundled (Zephyr SDK host tools, STM32CubeIDE) rather than as a standalone install. Treat any standalone host-OS claim as unverified until the guide's install/running chapters are fetched.

detection.detail: openocd --version on PATH — the standard probe, but the flag was not confirmed on a fetched official page in this pass (the User's Guide 'Running' chapter failed to fetch).
Bundled copy inside a Zephyr SDK install: OpenOCD ships as an SDK host tool (its udev rules file 60-openocd.rules sits under the SDK hosttools sysroot share/openocd/contrib/).
Bundled copy inside STM32CubeIDE: the v2.2.0 release note's bundle list includes an Open On-Chip Debugger component.

version_constraints.rule: No standalone OpenOCD version floor is stated on the fetched guide pages; bundled versions are per-consumer (e.g. STM32CubeIDE v2.2.0's bundle) and must not be generalised into a standalone requirement.

compatibility_rules.rule: Recommended ros_gz pairings: ROS 2 Jazzy <-> Gazebo Harmonic; ROS 2 Humble <-> Gazebo Fortress; ROS 2 Kilted <-> Gazebo Ionic; ROS 2 Lyrical/Rolling <-> Gazebo Jetty.
compatibility_rules.notes: Gazebo's official recommendation for new users: Ubuntu 24.04 + ROS 2 Jazzy + Gazebo Harmonic. Humble<->Harmonic is possible but non-official (needs ros-humble-ros-gzharmonic from OSRF and conflicts with ros-humble-ros-gz* packages).

compatibility_rules.rule: ROS 2 Jazzy is incompatible with Gazebo Fortress, Ionic and Jetty; ROS 2 Humble is incompatible with Gazebo Ionic and Jetty (official pairing table). A machine with Jazzy + Fortress is INCOMPATIBLE for a Jazzy stack even if both tools run.
compatibility_rules.notes: This is the compatibility rule the Phase 1 spec's example conflict (ros2:jazzy vs gazebo:fortress) anticipated; the official table confirms it.

compatibility_rules.rule: ROS 2 distro pairs with one Ubuntu LTS at Tier 1: Jazzy <-> Ubuntu 24.04, Humble <-> Ubuntu 22.04 (REP 2000). Other combinations are Tier 2/3 or unsupported.
compatibility_rules.notes: Windows 10 (VS2019) is also Tier 1 for both distros; macOS is Tier 3 only.

compatibility_rules.rule: For PX4 + ROS 2 work, PX4's supported/recommended platform is ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04; on Ubuntu 22.04 use ROS 2 Humble. ROS 2 apps must use px4_msgs matching the firmware's message definitions (message-versioning translation node exception from PX4 v1.16).
compatibility_rules.notes: Supersedes older PX4 doc versions that recommended Humble/22.04 as the primary pairing; always check the current (main) PX4 guide.

compatibility_rules.rule: PX4's dev environment installs Gazebo Harmonic by default; on Ubuntu 24.04, Gazebo Harmonic, Ionic and Jetty are supported with PX4. Modern Gazebo supersedes Gazebo Classic from Ubuntu 22.04 onwards.
compatibility_rules.notes: Interaction with the ros_gz pairing rule: if ROS 2 is also in the selection, the ROS pairing table governs which Gazebo belongs (Jazzy -> Harmonic).

compatibility_rules.rule: Docker Desktop on Windows requires WSL 2.1.5 or later, Windows 10 64-bit 22H2 (build 19045) or Windows 11 64-bit 23H2 (build 22631) or higher, a 64-bit processor with SLAT, hardware virtualisation enabled, and 8 GB system RAM.
compatibility_rules.notes: Docker Desktop is not supported on Windows Server. On Linux, Docker Engine is the native route; Desktop for Linux requires Ubuntu 26.04 or 24.04 LTS (x86-64).

compatibility_rules.rule: Official QGroundControl AppImages run on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and 26.04 LTS; on Ubuntu 22.04 QGC must be built from source (Stable V5.1 docs).
compatibility_rules.notes: Matters for stack targeting: a 22.04-based PX4 stack cannot assume a binary QGC install.

compatibility_rules.rule: Each Zephyr release has a recommended Zephyr SDK version, listed in the Zephyr SDK Version Compatibility Matrix; the matrix itself was not fetched in this pass, so no specific version pairings are asserted.
compatibility_rules.notes: The SDK docs page (fetched) defers to the matrix for the full list; fetch it before encoding any SDK-version rule.

stacks.name: PX4 Drone Development
targets: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (x86_64, arm64) — primary, ROS 2 Jazzy pairing
Ubuntu 22.04 LTS — supported with the ROS 2 Humble pairing

system_requirements.why: Floor carried from the Phase 1 spec sketch (the Omega-Ubuntu lesson: ~17 GB free cannot hold this stack); not an official vendor requirement.

members.constraints: Source checkout built locally; dev environment per PX4 docs for the target Ubuntu.
members.why: The autopilot itself — SITL and firmware builds are the capability this stack exists for.

members.constraints: Harmonic with ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04 (Fortress-era pairings do not apply here); on 22.04 PX4's setup installs Harmonic by default.
members.why: PX4 SITL's current default simulator, installed by PX4's own dev setup; a drone-development stack without its simulator cannot demonstrate flight.

members.constraints: Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04 (Humble on 22.04); px4_msgs must match the PX4 firmware's message definitions.
members.why: Required for this stack's ROS 2 integration capability (offboard control, companion-computer apps) — it is a stack requirement, not a PX4 requirement: PX4 alone flies without ROS 2, and a user who deselects ROS 2 keeps a valid PX4+Gazebo SITL selection.

members.constraints: Binary AppImages need Ubuntu 24.04+; on 22.04 it is build-from-source only.
members.why: Ground-station view, vehicle setup and log review for the SITL vehicle; SITL builds and runs without it.

members.constraints: Python package (pip) or C++ library; needs Python 3.8+ for the Python form.
members.why: Programmatic/offboard control experiments from Python or C++; a library you add per project, never needed for a basic SITL flight.

members.constraints: Operational means the daemon answers docker info, not just the CLI existing.
members.why: Alternative container route for PX4/simulator environments; the native dev setup does not need it.
Editor comfort only — PX4's docs suggest it as a next step; nothing in the stack depends on it.

members.constraints: Distro must pair with the OS: Jazzy on 24.04, Humble on 22.04 (REP 2000 Tier 1).
members.why: The middleware base everything else in this stack is a package of.

members.constraints: Nav2 build/binary must match the sourced ROS distro (navigation2 + nav2_bringup packages).
members.why: Autonomous navigation — planning, control and localization — is the stack's defining capability.

members.constraints: Version locked to the installed ROS distro; arrives via the ROS 2 installation, not a separate installer.
members.why: The standard visualisation/debugging surface for Nav2 (maps, plans, TF); without it the stack is effectively blind.

members.constraints: Must follow the ros_gz pairing for the selected distro (Jazzy->Harmonic, Humble->Fortress).
members.why: One simulator choice for developing against a virtual robot; a hardware-only user can drop the simulator group entirely and keep a valid stack.

members.constraints: Daemon must be running for Nav2's container route.
members.why: Nav2 publishes pre-built Docker images and dev containers as an alternative install route.
Editor comfort only.

members.constraints: Core (pio) standalone or bundled in the VS Code extension; frameworks are chosen per project in platformio.ini.
members.why: The lab's core: one build/upload/debug front-end across boards and frameworks, so projects — not the workstation — decide Arduino vs ESP-IDF vs vendor SDKs.

members.constraints: Espressif chips only; Python 3.11+ (current) and CMake 3.16+; install via EIM (current) or the legacy ~/esp/esp-idf flow.
members.why: The vendor-native ESP32 path: choose it standalone (EIM/Espressif IDE), or as the framework a PlatformIO project selects — one of the alternative ESP32 development paths, never an add-on forced on Arduino or STM32 work.

members.constraints: Board support via Board Manager packages; Linux form is an AppImage needing FUSE.
members.why: The beginner-friendly standalone IDE path for Arduino-core boards (including ESP32 cores); an alternative environment to PlatformIO/ESP-IDF, not a dependency of either.

members.constraints: Frequently arrives bundled (Zephyr SDK, STM32CubeIDE); a standalone copy is only needed for probe work outside those flows.
members.why: JTAG/SWD debug-probe server for hardware debugging across the lab's frameworks.

members.constraints: Host minimums: CMake 3.28.0, Python 3.12, devicetree compiler 1.4.6; SDK version should follow the Zephyr SDK compatibility matrix (unverified numbers).
members.why: The RTOS path: adds west-managed Zephyr development for supported boards when a project targets Zephyr.

members.constraints: 64-bit hosts only; ST's current documents disagree on exact Ubuntu/Fedora versions — pin claims to a CubeIDE release.
members.why: The vendor IDE for STM32 targets; only relevant when the lab works with STM32 hardware.
Hosts the recommended PlatformIO IDE extension route, but PlatformIO Core works without it.
